Problem 16.18 Lesson 30 · p. 1146 · §16.2

Noise margins and the width of the transition region from the VTC levels, then the supply needed for a required margin.

Problem statement

16.18 For a particular inverter design using a power supply VDD, VOL=0.1VDD, VOH=0.8VDD, VIL=0.25VDD, and VIH=0.6VDD. What are the noise margins? What is the width of the transition region? For a minimum noise margin of 0.25 V, what value of VDD is required?

No figure is referenced by this problem. The similar problem below uses the VTC of Fig. 16.13.

Similar to 16.18 same kind of inverter specification, new numbers · Fig. 16.13

Find both noise margins and the width of the transition region from fractions of the supply, then find the supply that gives a required minimum noise margin.

Similar problem (new numbers)

For a particular inverter design using a power supply VDD, VOL=0.10VDD, VOH=0.85VDD, VIL=0.40VDD, and VIH=0.70VDD. What are the noise margins? What is the width of the transition region? For a minimum noise margin of 0.30 V, what value of VDD is required?

Step 1 · Noise margin for low input

From Eq. (16.8), NML=VIL−VOL, with each level a fraction of VDD:

NML=0.40VDD−0.10VDD=0.30VDD
Step 2 · Noise margin for high input

From Eq. (16.9), NMH=VOH−VIH:

NMH=0.85VDD−0.70VDD=0.15VDD
Step 3 · Width of the transition region

Fig. 16.13 shows the transition region between VIL and VIH on the input axis, so its width is

VIH−VIL=0.70VDD−0.40VDD=0.30VDD
Step 4 · Supply for a required minimum noise margin

The smaller margin is NMH=0.15VDD, so it sets the minimum. Circuit rule: set the smaller margin equal to the target and solve for VDD:

0.15VDD=0.30V⇒VDD=0.300.15=2.0V

Check: at VDD=2.0 V, NML=0.60 V and NMH=0.30 V, so the minimum is 0.30 V as required.

Answers (similar problem)
NML0.30VDD
NMH0.15VDD
Width of transition region0.30VDD
VDD for minimum margin 0.30 V2.0 V

Lesson 30 notetaker: the CMOS inverter VTC, noise margins and asymmetry notetaker pp. 30-1 to 30-10
Summarized (class notetaker)

The lesson starts from the matched CMOS inverter of Fig. 16.22 (same threshold magnitude and equal kn and kp for the two transistors, so the widths are set by the ratio of the mobilities) and asks what basic shape the voltage-transfer characteristic should have. The notes add the input thresholds VIL and VIH to a vOUT versus vIN grid and recall how they relate to the two noise margins: NML=VIL−VOL and NMH=VOH−VIH. The standard way to define VIL and VIH is to require a slope of −1 on the VTC.

Next the notes mark the operating mode of each transistor along the curve. For the NMOS: cutoff when VGSN<Vt; saturation when VDSN≥VOV, that is VDSN≥VGSN−Vt; triode when VDSN<VGSN−Vt. The PMOS conditions are the mirror images written with VSGP and VSDP. With VGSN=vIN, VDSN=vOUT, VSGP=VDD−vIN and VSDP=VDD−vOUT, the mode conditions become inequalities between vOUT and vIN−Vt. The current equations come from Tables 5.1 and 5.2.

To find VIH the notes set IDN=IDP (NMOS in triode, PMOS in saturation), assume matched devices, differentiate both sides with respect to vIN (product and chain rules), set dvO/dvIN=−1 at vIN=VIH, substitute back and solve, reaching VIH=18(5VDD−2Vt). Symmetry about VDD/2 then gives VIL=18(3VDD+2Vt), and for a matched inverter the two noise margins are equal.

The notes then ask how far the midpoint VM moves if the transistors are not matched. At VM both devices are in saturation with vIN=vOUT=VM, so the notes again set IDN=IDP, take square roots and solve for VM, ending with the result in terms of r=kp/kn that the book prints as Eq. (16.39); they then assume VIL and VIH shift by about the same amount as VM. Pages 30-11 and 30-12 hold a worked class example that is not reproduced here.

Expansion note: why the two thresholds are defined by slope −1

On the flat parts of the VTC a small change at the input changes the output very little, so noise is absorbed. Where the curve reaches slope −1 the output starts to move as fast as the input, and the inverter stops cleaning up noise. That is why the book and the notes mark VIL and VIH at the two slope −1 points.

The voltage-transfer characteristic of a logic inverter §16.2.1, pp. 1121–1123; Fig. 16.13
Quoted · §16.2.1, p. 1122

With these observations in mind, we show in Fig. 16.13 a possible VTC of a logic inverter. For simplicity, we are using three straight lines to approximate the VTC, which is usually a nonlinear curve such as that in Fig. 16.12. Observe that the output high level, denoted VOH, does not depend on the exact value of vI as long as vI does not exceed the value labeled VIL; when vI exceeds VIL, the output decreases and the inverter enters its amplifier region of operation, also called the transition region. It follows that VIL is an important parameter of the inverter VTC: It is the maximum value that vI can have while being interpreted by the inverter as representing a logic 0.

Similarly, we observe that the output low level, denoted VOL, does not depend on the exact value of vI as long as vI does not fall below VIH. Thus VIH is an important parameter of the inverter VTC: It is the minimum value that vI can have while being interpreted by the inverter as representing a logic 1.

Noise margins and the critical points of the VTC §16.2.2, pp. 1122–1124; Eqs. (16.7)–(16.9); Table 16.1; Fig. 16.15
Quoted · §16.2.2, p. 1123

Here we assume that a noise or interference signal vN is somehow coupled to the interconnection between the output of inverter G1 and the input of inverter G2 with the result that the input of G2 becomes

vI2=vO1+vN
(16.7)

where the noise voltage vN can be either positive or negative. Now consider the case vO1=VOL; that is, inverter G2 is driven by a logic-0 signal. Reference to Fig. 16.13 indicates that in this case G2 will continue to function properly as long as its input vI2 does not exceed VIL. Equation (16.7) then indicates that vN can be as high as VIL−VOL while G2 continues to function properly. Thus, we can say that inverter G2 has a noise margin for low input, NML, of

NML=VIL−VOL
(16.8)

Similarly, if vO1=VOH, the driven inverter G2 will continue to see a high input as long as vI2 does not fall below VIH. Thus, in the high-input state, inverter G2 can tolerate a negative vN of magnitude as high as VOH−VIH. We can thus state that G2 has a high-input noise margin, NMH, of

NMH=VOH−VIH
(16.9)

In summary, four parameters, VOH, VOL, VIH, and VIL, define the VTC of an inverter and determine its noise margins, which in turn measure the ability of the inverter to tolerate variations in the input signal levels.

Expansion note: why there are two noise margins

A logic 0 and a logic 1 are each a range of voltages, and a noisy wire can push the level toward either edge of its range. The low-input margin measures how far a low signal can rise before the next gate stops reading it as 0; the high-input margin measures how far a high signal can fall before it stops reading as 1. The two can differ, and the smaller one limits the design.

Quoted · p. 1124

The formal definitions of the threshold voltages VIL and VIH are given in Fig. 16.15. Observe that VIL and VIH are defined as the VTC points at which the slope is −1 V/V. As vI exceeds VIL, the magnitude of the inverter gain increases and the VTC enters its transition region. Similarly, as vI falls below VIH, the inverter enters the transition region and the magnitude of the gain increases.

The ideal VTC §16.2.3, pp. 1124–1125; Fig. 16.16
Quoted · §16.2.3, pp. 1124–1125

An ideal VTC is one that maximizes the output signal swing and the noise margins. For an inverter operated from a power supply VDD, maximum signal swing is obtained when VOH=VDD and VOL=0.

To obtain maximum noise margins, we first arrange for the transition region to be made as narrow as possible and ideally of zero width. Then, the two noise margins are equalized by arranging for the transition from high to low to occur at the midpoint of the power supply, that is, at VDD/2. The result is the VTC shown in Fig. 16.16, for which VIL=VIH=VM=VDD/2.

Variables
SymbolMeaning
VDDPositive supply voltage
VOH, VOLOutput high and low levels of the inverter
VIH, VILMinimum input read as a logic 1; maximum input read as a logic 0 (the slope −1 points)
NMH, NMLNoise margins for high and low input
VMMidpoint of the VTC, where vO=vI
vI, vOInput and output voltages
vNNoise voltage added to a signal line

Problem 16.28 Lesson 30 · p. 1147 · §16.3

Matched CMOS inverter: PMOS width and silicon area, VTC levels and noise margins, and output resistance in each state.

Problem statement

16.28 Consider a CMOS inverter fabricated in a 65-nm CMOS process for which VDD=1 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.35 V, and μnCox=5.4μpCox=540 μA/V2. In addition, QN and QP have L=65 nm and (W/L)n=1.5.

  1. Find Wp that results in VM=VDD/2. What is the silicon area utilized by the inverter in this case?
  2. For the matched case in (a), find the values of VOH, VOL, VIH, VIL, NML, and NMH.
  3. For the matched case in (a), find the output resistance of the inverter in each of its two states.

No figure is referenced by this problem. The circuit is the CMOS inverter of Fig. 16.22, shown with the reading.

Similar to 16.28 same kind of inverter, new numbers · Fig. 16.22

Size the PMOS for a symmetric VTC, find the silicon area, the VTC levels and noise margins, and the output resistance in each state.

Similar problem (new numbers)

Consider a CMOS inverter fabricated in a 90-nm CMOS process for which VDD=1.1 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.30 V, and μnCox=3.5μpCox=420 μA/V2. In addition, QN and QP have L=90 nm and (W/L)n=2.

  1. Find Wp that results in VM=VDD/2. What is the silicon area utilized by the inverter in this case?
  2. For the matched case in (a), find the values of VOH, VOL, VIH, VIL, NML, and NMH.
  3. For the matched case in (a), find the output resistance of the inverter in each of its two states.
Step 1 · Width of the p-channel device

VM=VDD/2 requires matched devices, so Eq. (16.32) applies with equal lengths. The width of QN comes from its aspect ratio (units: W=(W/L)×L):

Wn=(W/L)nL=2×90=180nm
Wp=μnμpWn=3.5×180=630nm
Eq. (16.32)
Step 2 · Silicon area

Circuit rule: area of a rectangle, W×L for each transistor, added:

A=WnL+WpL=90(180+630)=72,900nm2
Step 3 · Output levels

The CMOS inverter swings fully between the rails (p. 1136, item 1): VOH=VDD=1.1 V and VOL=0.

Step 4 · Input thresholds

With Vt=0.30 V, Eqs. (16.35) and (16.36) give

VIH=18(5VDD−2Vt)=18(5.5−0.6)=0.6125V
VIL=18(3VDD+2Vt)=18(3.3+0.6)=0.4875V
Step 5 · Noise margins

From Eqs. (16.37) and (16.38):

NMH=VOH−VIH=1.1−0.6125=0.4875V,NML=VIL−VOL=0.4875V

The two margins are equal, as expected for a matched inverter.

Step 6 · Output resistance in each state

With QN on (output low), from Eq. (16.26), where kn′=μnCox=420 μA/V2 and VDD−Vtn=0.8 V:

rDSN=1kn′(W/L)n(VDD−Vtn)=1420×10−6×2×0.8=1488Ω

With QP on (output high), from Eq. (16.27), where kp′=420/3.5=120 μA/V2 and (W/L)p=630/90=7:

rDSP=1kp′(W/L)p(VDD−|Vtp|)=1120×10−6×7×0.8=1488Ω

The two resistances are equal because kn′(W/L)n=kp′(W/L)p=840 μA/V2.

Answers (similar problem)
Wn, Wp180 nm, 630 nm
Silicon area72,900 nm2
VOH, VOL1.1 V, 0
VIH, VIL0.6125 V, 0.4875 V
NMH, NML0.4875 V, 0.4875 V
rDSN, rDSP1488 Ω, 1488 Ω

Lesson 30 notetaker: the CMOS inverter VTC, noise margins and asymmetry notetaker pp. 30-1 to 30-10
Summarized (class notetaker)

The lesson starts from the matched CMOS inverter of Fig. 16.22 (same threshold magnitude and equal kn and kp for the two transistors, so the widths are set by the ratio of the mobilities) and asks what basic shape the voltage-transfer characteristic should have. The notes add the input thresholds VIL and VIH to a vOUT versus vIN grid and recall how they relate to the two noise margins: NML=VIL−VOL and NMH=VOH−VIH. The standard way to define VIL and VIH is to require a slope of −1 on the VTC.

Next the notes mark the operating mode of each transistor along the curve. For the NMOS: cutoff when VGSN<Vt; saturation when VDSN≥VOV, that is VDSN≥VGSN−Vt; triode when VDSN<VGSN−Vt. The PMOS conditions are the mirror images written with VSGP and VSDP. With VGSN=vIN, VDSN=vOUT, VSGP=VDD−vIN and VSDP=VDD−vOUT, the mode conditions become inequalities between vOUT and vIN−Vt. The current equations come from Tables 5.1 and 5.2.

To find VIH the notes set IDN=IDP (NMOS in triode, PMOS in saturation), assume matched devices, differentiate both sides with respect to vIN (product and chain rules), set dvO/dvIN=−1 at vIN=VIH, substitute back and solve, reaching VIH=18(5VDD−2Vt). Symmetry about VDD/2 then gives VIL=18(3VDD+2Vt), and for a matched inverter the two noise margins are equal.

The notes then ask how far the midpoint VM moves if the transistors are not matched. At VM both devices are in saturation with vIN=vOUT=VM, so the notes again set IDN=IDP, take square roots and solve for VM, ending with the result in terms of r=kp/kn that the book prints as Eq. (16.39); they then assume VIL and VIH shift by about the same amount as VM. Pages 30-11 and 30-12 hold a worked class example that is not reproduced here.

Expansion note: why the two thresholds are defined by slope −1

On the flat parts of the VTC a small change at the input changes the output very little, so noise is absorbed. Where the curve reaches slope −1 the output starts to move as fast as the input, and the inverter stops cleaning up noise. That is why the book and the notes mark VIL and VIH at the two slope −1 points.

CMOS inverter operation and its output resistance §16.3.1, pp. 1134–1136; Figs. 16.22–16.24; Eqs. (16.26), (16.27)
Quoted · §16.3.1, p. 1134

We first consider the two extreme cases: when vI is at logic-0 level, which is 0 V, and when vI is at logic-1 level, which is VDD volts. In both cases, for ease of exposition we shall consider the n-channel device QN to be the driving transistor and the p-channel device QP to be the load. However, since the circuit is symmetric, this assumption is obviously arbitrary, and the reverse would lead to identical results.

Figure 16.23 illustrates the case when vI=VDD … Since vSGP<|Vt|, the load curve will be a horizontal straight line at zero current level. The operating point will be at the intersection of the two curves, where we note that the output voltage is zero and the current through the two devices is also zero. This means that the power dissipation in the circuit is zero. Note, however, that although QN is operating at zero current and zero drain-source voltage (i.e., at the origin of the iD–vDS plane), the operating point is on a steep segment of the iD–vDS characteristic curve. Thus QN provides a low-resistance path between the output terminal and ground, with the resistance obtained using Eq. (5.13b) as

rDSN=1/[kn′(WL)n(VDD−Vtn)]
(16.26)
Quoted · p. 1135

Figure 16.24(c) shows the equivalent circuit of the inverter when the input is low. Here we see that QP provides a low-resistance path between the output terminal and the dc supply VDD, with the resistance given by

rDSP=1/[kp′(WL)p(VDD−|Vtp|)]
(16.27)

The equivalent circuit confirms that in this case vO≡VOH=VDD and that the power dissipation in the inverter is zero.

[Footnote, p. 1134] In Section 16.1 we referred to rDSN (and rDSP for p-channel devices) as Ron.

Quoted · p. 1136

From the above, we conclude that the basic CMOS logic inverter behaves as an ideal inverter. In summary: 1. The output voltage levels are 0 and VDD, and thus the signal swing is the maximum possible. This, coupled with the fact that the inverter can be designed to provide a symmetrical voltage-transfer characteristic, results in wide noise margins. … 3. A low-resistance path exists between the output terminal and ground (in the low-output state) or VDD (in the high-output state). These low-resistance paths ensure that the output voltage is 0 or VDD independent of the exact values of the W/L ratios or other device parameters.

Expansion note: "output resistance" in a logic inverter

In a steady logic state one transistor is on and is working near the origin of its curve, where it acts like a plain resistor between the output and a supply or ground. That resistance is what the book calls rDSN or rDSP, and it is the resistance the inverter presents to whatever it drives in that state.

The complete CMOS VTC: currents, critical points and noise margins §16.3.2, pp. 1136–1139; Eqs. (16.28)–(16.38); Fig. 16.25
Quoted · §16.3.2, pp. 1136–1137

The complete voltage-transfer characteristic (VTC) of the CMOS inverter can be obtained by repeating the graphical procedure, used above in the two extreme cases, for all intermediate values of vI. In the following, we shall calculate the critical points of the resulting voltage-transfer curve. For this we need the i–v relationships of QN and QP. For QN,

iDN=kn′(WL)n[(vI−Vtn)vO−12vO2]for vO≤vI−Vtn
(16.28)
iDN=12kn′(WL)n(vI−Vtn)2for vO≥vI−Vtn
(16.29)

For QP,

iDP=kp′(WL)p[(VDD−vI−|Vtp|)(VDD−vO)−12(VDD−vO)2]for vO≥vI+|Vtp|
(16.30)
iDP=12kp′(WL)p(VDD−vI−|Vtp|)2for vO≤vI+|Vtp|
(16.31)

The CMOS inverter is usually designed to have Vtn=|Vtp|=Vt. Also, although this is not always the case, we shall assume that QN and QP are matched; that is, kn′(W/L)n=kp′(W/L)p. It should be noted that since μp is often 0.25 to 0.5 times the value of μn, to make k′(W/L) of the two devices equal, the width of the p-channel device is made two to four times that of the n-channel device. More specifically, the two devices are designed to have equal lengths, with widths related by

WpWn=μnμp
(16.32)

This will result in kn′(W/L)n=kp′(W/L)p, and the inverter will have a symmetric transfer characteristic and equal current-driving capability in both directions (pull-up and pull-down).

Quoted · pp. 1137–1139

With QN and QP matched, the CMOS inverter has the voltage-transfer characteristic shown in Fig. 16.25. As indicated, the transfer characteristic has five distinct segments corresponding to different combinations of modes of operation of QN and QP. The vertical segment BC is obtained when both QN and QP are operating in the saturation region. … From symmetry, this vertical segment occurs at vI=VDD/2 and is bounded by vO(B)=VDD/2+Vt, at which value QP enters the triode region and vO(C)=VDD/2−Vt, at which value QN enters the triode region.

The reader will recall from Section 16.2.1 that in addition to VOL and VOH, two other points on the transfer curve determine the noise margins of the inverter. These are the maximum permitted logic-0 or "low" level at the input, VIL, and the minimum permitted logic-1 or "high" level at the input, VIH. These are formally defined as the two points on the transfer curve at which the incremental gain is unity (i.e., the slope is −1 V/V).

To determine VIH, we note that QN is in the triode region, and thus its current is given by Eq. (16.28), while QP is in saturation and its current is given by Eq. (16.31). Equating iDN and iDP, and assuming matched devices, gives

(vI−Vt)vO−12vO2=12(VDD−vI−Vt)2
(16.33)

Differentiating both sides relative to vI results in

(vI−Vt)dvOdvI+vO−vOdvOdvI=−(VDD−vI−Vt)

in which we substitute vI=VIH and dvO/dvI=−1 to obtain

vO=VIH−VDD2
(16.34)

Substituting vI=VIH and for vO from Eq. (16.34) in Eq. (16.33) gives

VIH=18(5VDD−2Vt)
(16.35)

VIL can be determined in a manner similar to that used to find VIH. Alternatively, we can use the symmetry relationship

VIH−VDD2=VDD2−VIL

together with VIH from Eq. (16.35) to obtain

VIL=18(3VDD+2Vt)
(16.36)

The noise margins can now be determined as follows:

NMH=VOH−VIH=VDD−18(5VDD−2Vt)=18(3VDD+2Vt)
(16.37)
NML=VIL−VOL=18(3VDD+2Vt)−0=18(3VDD+2Vt)
(16.38)

As expected, the symmetry of the voltage-transfer characteristic results in equal noise margins. Of course, if QN and QP are not matched, the voltage-transfer characteristic will no longer be symmetric, and the noise margins will not be equal.

Expansion note: where the symbol Vt comes from

For the matched inverter Vtn=|Vtp|, and the book writes the common magnitude as Vt. In Eqs. (16.33) to (16.38) Vt is therefore the threshold magnitude of either transistor.

Expansion note: "matched" versus a symmetric VTC

Matched means the two devices have equal k (equal k′(W/L)) as well as equal threshold magnitude. Because μp is smaller than μn, equal k takes a wider PMOS, which is the content of Eq. (16.32). The resulting VTC is symmetric about VDD/2.

When Q_N and Q_P are not matched §16.3.3, p. 1139; Eqs. (16.39), (16.40)
Quoted · §16.3.3, p. 1139

The price paid for obtaining a perfectly symmetric VTC is that the width of the p-channel device can be three to four times as large as that of the n-channel device. This can result in a relatively large silicon area, which, besides being wasteful of silicon real estate, can also result in increased device capacitances and a corresponding increase in the propagation delay of the inverter (Section 17.1). It is useful, therefore, to inquire into the effect of not matching QN and QP. …

Since at M, both QN and QP operate in saturation, their currents are given by Eqs. (16.29) and (16.31), respectively. Substituting vI=vO=VM, and equating the two currents results in

VM=r(VDD−|Vtp|)+Vtnr+1
(16.39)

where

r=kpkn=μpWpμnWn
(16.40)

where we have assumed that QN and QP have the same channel length L, which is usually the case with L equal to the minimum available for the given process technology. Note that the matched case corresponds to r=1. For |Vtp|=Vtn, and r=1, Eq. (16.39) yields VM=VDD/2, as expected. … We make the following two observations: 1. VM increases with r. Thus, making kp>kn shifts VM toward VDD. Conversely, making kp<kn shifts VM toward 0. 2. VM is not a strong function of r. For the particular case shown, lowering r by a factor of 2 (from 1 to 0.5), reduces VM by only 0.05 V.

Expansion note: when Eq. (16.39) is needed

Eq. (16.39) describes a switching point when the two transistors are not matched. For a matched inverter the matching condition Eq. (16.32) sets the widths, and VM=VDD/2 follows from it.

Propagation delays by the method of average currents, and the theoretical maximum operating frequency.

Problem statement

17.14 Use the method of average currents to estimate tPHL, tPLH, and tP of a CMOS inverter fabricated in a 65-nm process for which Vtn=|Vtp|=0.35 V, VDD=1 V, μnCox=470 μA/V2, and μpCox=190 μA/V2. The inverter has (W/L)n=1.5 and (W/L)p=3, and the total capacitance at the inverter output node is 10 fF. Also, find the theoretical maximum frequency at which this inverter can be operated.

No figure is referenced by this problem. Fig. 17.4, which the reading uses for this inverter, is shown in the reading panels.

Similar problem (new numbers)

Use the method of average currents to estimate tPHL, tPLH, and tP of a CMOS inverter fabricated in a process for which Vtn=|Vtp|=0.40 V, VDD=1.1 V, μnCox=520 μA/V2, and μpCox=210 μA/V2. The inverter has (W/L)n=2 and (W/L)p=4, and the total capacitance at the inverter output node is 8 fF. Also, find the theoretical maximum frequency at which this inverter can be operated.

Step 1 · The factor an (and ap)

With Vtn/VDD=0.40/1.1=0.3636, Eq. (17.9) gives

an=27/4−3(0.3636)+(0.3636)2=20.7913=2.527

Since |Vtp|=Vtn, Eq. (17.11) gives ap=an=2.527.

Step 2 · Device transconductance parameters

Using k′=μCox and k=k′(W/L):

kn=520×2=1040μA/V2,kp=210×4=840μA/V2
Step 3 · High-to-low delay

From Eq. (17.8):

Step 4 · Low-to-high delay

From Eq. (17.10):

From Eq. (17.1):

tP=12(tPHL+tPLH)=12(17.67+21.88)=19.8ps
Step 6 · Theoretical maximum frequency

From p. 1178, f=1/(2tP):

fmax=12×19.78×10−12=25.3GHz

Check: an lies in the 1-to-3 range the book states, and tPLH>tPHL because QP is not fully matched to QN (840 < 1040 μA/V2).

Lesson 31 notetaker: propagation delay by average current and by equivalent resistance notetaker pp. 31-1 to 31-12
Summarized (class notetaker)

The lesson defines the delay measures first. The propagation delay is measured from the midpoint of the input transition to the point where the output passes the midpoint 12(VOL+VOH) of its swing; tPHL is the delay for a falling output and tPLH for a rising output. Rise and fall times run between the 10% and 90% points of an edge, and the transition times tTHL and tTLH are the output's own 90%-to-10% and 10%-to-90% times.

Method 1, average current. All the capacitances at the output are replaced by one capacitor C to ground. For the falling edge, QP turns off and QN turns on, and the output falls from VDD to VDD/2. On the QN characteristic the operating point starts at point E (saturation, vGSN=VDD) and slides to point M (triode, vDSN=VDD/2). The notes evaluate the saturation current at E and the triode current at M, take their average as a constant discharge current, and apply ΔQ=CΔV with ΔV=VDD/2. Factoring out VDD2 gives tPHL=anC/(KnVDD) with an set by Vtn/VDD, and the same steps with QP give tPLH with ap. When QN and QP are matched the two delays are about equal.

Method 2, equivalent resistance. Each transistor is modelled as a resistor charging or discharging C through a first-order RC response. Setting the output equal to VDD/2 gives t=RCln2≈0.693RC, so tPHL=0.693RNC and tPLH=0.693RPC. The effective resistances are measured at a convenient Weff/Leff and scaled to the actual aspect ratio.

The load capacitance. The notes split C into an internal part (gate-drain capacitances counted twice by the Miller effect, plus the drain-body capacitances) and an external part per driven gate (wire plus the gate capacitances of the load inverter), multiplied by the fan-out. The notetaker's class example is a different problem from the assigned ones and is not reproduced here.

Expansion note: why the two methods give similar but not identical answers

Method 1 builds the delay from the transistor current equations; Method 2 replaces each transistor by one resistance measured from simulation or experiment. The second therefore includes effects the hand equations ignore (such as velocity saturation, which the book mentions on p. 1157), so the two results are close but not equal.

Propagation delay: definitions §17.1.1, pp. 1150–1154; Eqs. (17.1), (17.2); Fig. 17.1
Quoted · §17.1.1, p. 1151

… There is a time delay between each edge of the input pulse and the corresponding change in the output of the inverter. If we define the "switching point" of the output as the time at which the output pulse passes through the half-point of its excursion, then we can define the propagation delays of the inverter as indicated in Fig. 17.1(b). Note that there are two propagation delays, which are not necessarily equal: the propagation delay for the output going from high to low, tPHL, and the propagation delay for the output going from low to high, tPLH. The inverter propagation delay tP is defined as the average of the two,

tP≡12(tPLH+tPHL)
(17.1)

At this point, you are likely wondering about the cause of the finite propagation time of the inverter. It is simply a result of the time needed to charge and discharge the various capacitances in the circuit. These include the MOSFET capacitances, the wiring capacitance, and the input capacitances of all the logic gates driven by the inverter. … A fundamental relationship in analyzing the dynamic operation of a circuit is

IΔt=ΔQ=CΔV
(17.2)

That is, a current I flowing through a capacitance C for an interval Δt deposits a charge ΔQ on the capacitor, which causes the capacitor voltage to increase by ΔV.

Expansion note: "propagation delay" versus "transition time"

A propagation delay (like tPHL) says when the output edge arrives, measured at the half-way points of the input and output edges. A transition time says how long the output edge itself takes between its 10% and 90% points. The book defines them together in Fig. 17.3 and uses the delays in everything that follows.

Propagation delay of the CMOS inverter by the method of average currents §17.1.2, pp. 1154–1157; Eqs. (17.4)–(17.11); Fig. 17.4
Quoted · §17.1.2, pp. 1154–1155

Our strategy for determining the propagation delay of the CMOS inverter consists of two steps: 1. Replace all the capacitances in the circuit; that is, the various capacitances associated with QN and QP, the capacitance of the wire that connects the output of the inverter to other circuits, and the input capacitance of the logic gates the inverter drives, by a single equivalent capacitance C connected between the output node of the inverter and ground. 2. Analyze the resulting capacitively loaded inverter to determine its tPLH and tPHL, and hence tP.

Just prior to the leading edge of the input pulse (i.e., at t=0−), the output voltage is equal to VDD and capacitor C is charged to this voltage. At t=0, vI rises to VDD, causing QP to turn off and QN to turn on. From then on, the circuit is equivalent to that shown in Fig. 17.4(c), with the initial value of vO=VDD. Thus, at t=0+, QN will operate in the saturation region and will supply a relatively large current to begin the process of discharging C. … Here we are interested in the interval tPHL during which vO reduces from VDD to VDD/2. Correspondingly, the operating point of QN moves from E to M. For a portion of this time, corresponding to the segment EF of the trajectory, QN operates in saturation. Then at F, vO=VDD−Vt, and QN enters the triode region.

A simple approach for determining tPHL consists of first calculating the average value of the current supplied by QN over the segment EM. Then, we use this average value of the discharge current to approximate tPHL by means of the charge balance equation IavtPHL=C[VDD−(VDD/2)] resulting in

tPHL=CVDD2Iav
(17.4)

The value of Iav can be found as follows:

Iav=12[iDN(E)+iDN(M)]
(17.5)

where

iDN(E)=12kn′(WL)n(VDD−Vtn)2
(17.6)

and

iDN(M)=kn′(WL)n[(VDD−Vtn)(VDD2)−12(VDD2)2]
(17.7)

Note that we have assumed λn=0. Combining Eqs. (17.4) to (17.7) provides

tPHL=anCkn′(W/L)nVDD
(17.8)

where an is a factor determined by the relative values of Vt and VDD;

an=2/[74−3VtnVDD+(VtnVDD)2]
(17.9)

The value of an typically falls in the range of 1 to 3.

An expression for the low-to-high inverter delay, tPLH, can be written by analogy to the tPHL expression in Eq. (17.8),

tPLH=apCkp′(W/L)pVDD
(17.10)

where

ap=2/[74−3|Vtp|VDD+(|Vtp|VDD)2]
(17.11)

Finally, the propagation delay tP can be found as the average of tPHL and tPLH, as in Eq. (17.1).

Quoted · p. 1157

Examination of the formulas in Eqs. (17.8) to (17.11) enables us to make a number of useful observations: 1. As expected, the two components of tP can be equalized by selecting the (W/L) ratios to equalize kn and kp, that is, by matching QN and QP. This assumes that an=ap, which is obtained when Vtn=−Vtp. 2. Since tP is proportional to C, the designer should strive to reduce C. … 4. Using larger W/L ratios can result in a reduction in tP. Care should be taken here, however, since increasing the size of the devices increases the value of C, so that the expected reduction in tP might not be possible. …

Expansion note: where the 7/4 in an comes from

It is just the algebra of averaging the two currents. Adding the saturation current at E and the triode current at M, dividing by CVDD/2 and collecting terms leaves the bracketed expression in Eq. (17.9). The class notes expand it step by step, and the book prints only the final factor.

Expansion note: kn versus kn′

The book writes kn′(W/L)n in Eq. (17.8). The product of the process parameter kn′=μnCox and the aspect ratio is the device parameter kn, which the class notes call Kn.

Expansion note: use |Vtp| in ap

The PMOS threshold voltage is negative, so Eq. (17.11) is written with its magnitude. Only positive quantities go into ap.

Worked example in the reading: Example 17.2 (average-current part) Example 17.2, pp. 1159–1160
Quoted · Example 17.2, p. 1159

Example 17.2 Determining the Propagation Delay of the CMOS Inverter. For a 65-nm process characterized by VDD=1.0 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.35 V, kn′=5.4kp′=540 μA/V2, find tPLH, tPHL, and tP for an inverter for which (W/L)n=1.5 and (W/L)p=3, and for C=5 fF. In this technology, transistors with (W/L)=1.5 are found to have Reff,N=8 kΩ and Reff,P=24 kΩ. Use both the approach based on average currents and the one based on equivalent resistances, and compare your results. …

(a) Using the average current approach, we determine, from Eq. (17.9), an=2/[7/4−3(0.35/1.0)+(0.35/1.0)2]=2.43 and using Eq. (17.8), tPHL=2.43×5×10−15/(540×10−6×1.5×1.0)=15.0 ps. Since |Vtp|=Vtn, ap=an=2.43 and we can determine tPLH from Eq. (17.10) as tPLH=2.43×5×10−15/[(540/5.4)×10−6×3×1.0]=40.5 ps. The propagation delay can now be found as tP=12(tPHL+tPLH)=12(15.0+40.5)=27.8 ps.

Expansion note: how the example reads the process parameters

The statement gives kn′ and the ratio kn′/kp′, so the example computes kp′=540/5.4=100 μA/V2 inline, as you can see in its tPLH line.

Related exercise in the reading Exercise 17.4, p. 1161
Related exercise in the reading · p. 1161

17.4 For a CMOS inverter fabricated in a 0.18-μm process with VDD=1.8 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.5 V, kn′=4kp′=300 μA/V2, and having (W/L)n=1.5 and (W/L)p=3, find tPHL, tPLH, and tP when the equivalent load capacitance C=10 fF. Use the method of average currents.

Book answers: 24.8 ps; 49.6 ps; 37.2 ps

Maximum switching frequency §17.3.2, p. 1178; Eq. (17.43)
Quoted · §17.3.2, p. 1178

If the inverter is operated at its theoretical maximum switching speed determined as f=12tP [as printed; the context, PDP=fCVDD2tP=12CVDD2, shows the intended f=1/(2tP)], then PDP=12CVDD2 (17.43).

Expansion note: why a period of 2tP

One full cycle of the input has a rising edge and a falling edge. The output needs about tPHL after one edge and tPLH after the other, which is about 2tP in total, so the highest rate at which the inverter can be toggled is one cycle per 2tP.

Problem 17.15 Lesson 31 · p. 1186 · §17.1

Average-current propagation delay when the capacitance scales with device width, then the delay of the matched design.

Problem statement

17.15 Find the propagation delay for an inverter for which kn′=4kp′=500 μA/V2 and (W/L)n=(W/L)p=130 nm/65 nm, VDD=1.0 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.35 V, and the capacitance is roughly 2.5 fF/μm of device width. There is an additional load capacitance of 2 fF. What does tP become if the design is changed to a matched one? Use the method of average current.

No figure is referenced by this problem. Fig. 17.4, which the reading uses for this inverter, is shown in the reading panels.

Similar to 17.15 same method, new numbers · Fig. 17.4

Average-current propagation delay of an inverter whose capacitance depends on its device widths, then the delay after changing to a matched design.

Similar problem (new numbers)

Find the propagation delay for an inverter for which kn′=4kp′=400 μA/V2 and (W/L)n=(W/L)p=150 nm/50 nm, VDD=1.2 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.40 V, and the capacitance is roughly 2.0 fF/μm of device width. There is an additional load capacitance of 3 fF. What does tP become if the design is changed to a matched one? Use the method of average current.

Step 1 · Total capacitance of the given design

Reading the statement (an interpretation, not stated in the book): the capacitance of the inverter is taken as 2.0 fF per micrometre of the combined width of QN and QP, and the load adds in parallel (circuit rule: capacitances at one node add).

C=2.0fF/μm×(0.150+0.150)μm+3fF=3.60fF
Step 2 · Delay factor

Vt/VDD=0.40/1.2=1/3. From Eq. (17.9), with |Vtp|=Vtn so ap=an:

an=27/4−3(1/3)+(1/3)2=20.8611=2.323
Step 3 · Device parameters

(W/L)=150/50=3 for both. With kp′=400/4=100 μA/V2:

kn=400×3=1200μA/V2,kp=100×3=300μA/V2
Step 4 · Delays of the given design

From Eqs. (17.8), (17.10) and (17.1):

tPHL=2.323×3.6×10−151200×10−6×1.2=5.81ps,tPLH=2.323×3.6×10−15300×10−6×1.2=23.2ps
tP=12(5.81+23.23)=14.5ps
Step 5 · The matched design

Matching needs kn=kp with equal lengths, so by Eq. (16.32) Wp/Wn=μn/μp=kn′/kp′=4. Keep Wn=150 nm, so Wp=600 nm and (W/L)p=12. The device capacitance grows with the width:

C=2.0×(0.150+0.600)+3=4.50fF
kp=100×12=1200μA/V2=kn
Step 6 · Delay of the matched design

Now tPHL=tPLH (same a, same k):

tPHL=tPLH=2.323×4.5×10−151200×10−6×1.2=7.26ps=tP

The delay is cut by about a factor of 2 even though the capacitance grew by 25%, because QP now supplies four times the current.

tPHL, tPLH, tP (given design)5.81 ps, 23.2 ps, 14.5 ps
Wp (matched)600 nm
C (matched)4.50 fF
tP (matched)7.26 ps

Propagation delay: definitions §17.1.1, pp. 1150–1154; Eqs. (17.1), (17.2); Fig. 17.1
Quoted · §17.1.1, p. 1151

… There is a time delay between each edge of the input pulse and the corresponding change in the output of the inverter. If we define the "switching point" of the output as the time at which the output pulse passes through the half-point of its excursion, then we can define the propagation delays of the inverter as indicated in Fig. 17.1(b). IΔt=ΔQ=CΔV
(17.2)

That is, a current I flowing through a capacitance C for an interval Δt deposits a charge ΔQ on the capacitor, which causes the capacitor voltage to increase by ΔV.

Expansion note: "propagation delay" versus "transition time"

A propagation delay (like tPHL) says when the output edge arrives, measured at the half-way points of the input and output edges. A transition time says how long the output edge itself takes between its 10% and 90% points. The book defines them together in Fig. 17.3 and uses the delays in everything that follows.

Propagation delay of the CMOS inverter by the method of average currents §17.1.2, pp. 1154–1157; Eqs. (17.4)–(17.11); Fig. 17.4
Quoted · §17.1.2, pp. 1154–1155

Our strategy for determining the propagation delay of the CMOS inverter consists of two steps: 1. Replace all the capacitances in the circuit; that is, the various capacitances associated with QN and QP, the capacitance of the wire that connects the output of the inverter to other circuits, and the input capacitance of the logic gates the inverter drives, by a single equivalent capacitance C connected between the output node of the inverter and ground. 2. Analyze the resulting capacitively loaded inverter to determine its tPLH and tPHL, and hence tP.

Just prior to the leading edge of the input pulse (i.e., at t=0−), the output voltage is equal to VDD and capacitor C is charged to this voltage. At t=0, vI rises to VDD, causing QP to turn off and QN to turn on. From then on, the circuit is equivalent to that shown in Fig. 17.4(c), with the initial value of vO=VDD. Thus, at t=0+, QN will operate in the saturation region and will supply a relatively large current to begin the process of discharging C. … Here we are interested in the interval tPHL during which vO reduces from VDD to VDD/2. Correspondingly, the operating point of QN moves from E to M. For a portion of this time, corresponding to the segment EF of the trajectory, QN operates in saturation. Then at F, vO=VDD−Vt, and QN enters the triode region.

A simple approach for determining tPHL consists of first calculating the average value of the current supplied by QN over the segment EM. Then, we use this average value of the discharge current to approximate tPHL by means of the charge balance equation IavtPHL=C[VDD−(VDD/2)] resulting in

tPHL=CVDD2Iav
(17.4)

The value of Iav can be found as follows:

Iav=12[iDN(E)+iDN(M)]
(17.5)

where

iDN(E)=12kn′(WL)n(VDD−Vtn)2
(17.6)

and

iDN(M)=kn′(WL)n[(VDD−Vtn)(VDD2)−12(VDD2)2]
(17.7)

Note that we have assumed λn=0. Combining Eqs. (17.4) to (17.7) provides

tPHL=anCkn′(W/L)nVDD
(17.8)

where an is a factor determined by the relative values of Vt and VDD;

an=2/[74−3VtnVDD+(VtnVDD)2]
(17.9)

The value of an typically falls in the range of 1 to 3.

An expression for the low-to-high inverter delay, tPLH, can be written by analogy to the tPHL expression in Eq. (17.8),

tPLH=apCkp′(W/L)pVDD
(17.10)

where

ap=2/[74−3|Vtp|VDD+(|Vtp|VDD)2]
(17.11)

Finally, the propagation delay tP can be found as the average of tPHL and tPLH, as in Eq. (17.1).

Quoted · p. 1157

Examination of the formulas in Eqs. (17.8) to (17.11) enables us to make a number of useful observations: 1. As expected, the two components of tP can be equalized by selecting the (W/L) ratios to equalize kn and kp, that is, by matching QN and QP. This assumes that an=ap, which is obtained when Vtn=−Vtp. 2. Since tP is proportional to C, the designer should strive to reduce C. … 4. Using larger W/L ratios can result in a reduction in tP. Care should be taken here, however, since increasing the size of the devices increases the value of C, so that the expected reduction in tP might not be possible. …

Expansion note: where the 7/4 in an comes from

It is just the algebra of averaging the two currents. Adding the saturation current at E and the triode current at M, dividing by CVDD/2 and collecting terms leaves the bracketed expression in Eq. (17.9). The class notes expand it step by step, and the book prints only the final factor.

Expansion note: kn versus kn′

The book writes kn′(W/L)n in Eq. (17.8). The product of the process parameter kn′=μnCox and the aspect ratio is the device parameter kn, which the class notes call Kn.

Expansion note: use |Vtp| in ap

The PMOS threshold voltage is negative, so Eq. (17.11) is written with its magnitude. Only positive quantities go into ap.

Determining the equivalent load capacitance C §17.1.3, pp. 1161–1163; Figs. 17.6, 17.7; Eqs. (17.18), (17.19)
Quoted · §17.1.3, p. 1162

… Let's now consider the contribution of each of the capacitances in Fig. 17.6 to the value of the equivalent load capacitance C: 1. The gate-drain overlap capacitance of Q1, Cgd1, can be replaced by an equivalent capacitance between the output node and ground of 2Cgd1. The factor 2 arises because of the Miller effect (Section 10.2). … The same applies for the gate-drain overlap capacitance of Q2, Cgd2, which is replaced by a capacitance 2Cgd2 between the output node and ground. 2. Each of the drain-body capacitances Cdb1 and Cdb2 has a terminal at a constant voltage. Thus for the purpose of our analysis here, Cdb1 and Cdb2 can be replaced with equal capacitances between the output node and ground. … 3. Since the second inverter does not switch states, we assume that the input capacitances of Q3 and Q4 remain approximately constant and equal to the total gate capacitance (WLCox+Cgsov+Cgdov). That is, the input capacitance of the load inverter will be

Cg3+Cg4=(WL)3Cox+(WL)4Cox+Cgsov3+Cgdov3+Cgsov4+Cgdov4
(17.18)

4. The last component of C is the wiring capacitance Cw, which simply adds to the value of C. Thus, the total value of C is given by

C=2Cgd1+2Cgd2+Cdb1+Cdb2+Cg3+Cg4+Cw
(17.19)
Expansion note: capacitances at one node add

All these capacitors are connected between the same output node and ground, so they are in parallel and their values simply add. That is why Eq. (17.19) is a plain sum once each capacitor has been converted to its equivalent value at the output node.

Related exercise in the reading Exercise 17.4, p. 1161
Related exercise in the reading · p. 1161

17.4 For a CMOS inverter fabricated in a 0.18-μm process with VDD=1.8 V, Vtn=−Vtp=0.5 V, kn′=4kp′=300 μA/V2, and having (W/L)n=1.5 and (W/L)p=3, find tPHL, tPLH, and tP when the equivalent load capacitance C=10 fF. Use the method of average currents.

Book answers: 24.8 ps; 49.6 ps; 37.2 ps

Problem 17.26 Lesson 31 · p. 1188 · §17.3

Energy per switching cycle, chip-level dynamic power and average supply current for a load capacitance charged and discharged by CMOS inverters.

Problem statement

17.26 An IC inverter fabricated in a 65-nm CMOS process is found to have a load capacitance of 3 fF. If the inverter is operated from a 1.2-V power supply, find the energy needed to charge and discharge the load capacitance. If the IC chip has 5 million of these inverters operating at an average switching frequency of 2.5 GHz, what is the power dissipated in the chip? What is the average current drawn from the power supply?

No figure is referenced by this problem. Fig. 17.12, the switch-level inverter model the reading uses, is shown in the reading panels.

Similar to 17.26 same quantities, new numbers · Fig. 17.12

Energy per charge-discharge cycle, dynamic power of a chip of many inverters, and the average supply current.

Similar problem (new numbers)

An IC inverter fabricated in a 90-nm CMOS process is found to have a load capacitance of 4 fF. If the inverter is operated from a 1.0-V power supply, find the energy needed to charge and discharge the load capacitance. If the IC chip has 500 thousand of these inverters operating at an average switching frequency of 1.5 GHz, what is the power dissipated in the chip? What is the average current drawn from the power supply?

Step 1 · Energy for one charge-discharge cycle

From Eq. (17.38), the energy dissipated per cycle is CVDD2 (half in the pull-up path while charging, half in the pull-down path while discharging):

E=CVDD2=4×10−15×(1.0)2=4.0fJ
Step 2 · Dynamic power of one inverter

From Eq. (17.39):

Pdyn=fCVDD2=1.5×109×4.0×10−15=6.0μW
Step 3 · Power of the whole chip

Circuit rule: powers of the individual inverters add, so with N=5×105:

Pchip=NPdyn=5×105×6.0μW=3.0W
Step 4 · Average supply current

Circuit rule: P=VI for the supply, so

I=PchipVDD=3.01.0=3.0A

Check by units: fJ times GHz is μW, and W divided by V is A.

Answers (similar problem)
Energy per cycle4.0 fJ
Power per inverter6.0 μW
Chip power3.0 W
Average supply current3.0 A

Formula toolkit 17.26

Given: the load capacitance, the supply voltage, the number of inverters and the average switching frequency. Nothing about the transistors is needed.

Eqs. (17.36), (17.37)

Lesson 31 context for this problem notetaker pp. 31-1 to 31-12
Summarized (class notetaker)

The Lesson 31 notes derive the propagation delay and the load capacitance C that an inverter charges and discharges. This problem uses a load capacitance the same way but asks about the energy and power of charging and discharging it, which the book treats in §17.3.1. The notes introduce C as the lumped capacitor from the output node to ground, made of internal and external parts. The notes do not derive the power formulas.

Dynamic power dissipation of the CMOS inverter §17.3.1, pp. 1174–1176; Fig. 17.12; Eqs. (17.34)–(17.39)
Quoted · §17.3.1, pp. 1174–1175

… as the inverter is switched from one state to another, current must flow through the switch(es) to charge (and discharge) the load capacitance. These currents give rise to power dissipation in the switches, called dynamic power dissipation.

An expression for the dynamic power dissipation of the inverter of Fig. 17.12(a) can be derived as follows. Consider first the situation when vI goes low. The pull-down switch PD turns off and the pull-up switch PU turns on. In this state, the inverter can be represented by the equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 17.12(b). Capacitor C will charge through the on-resistance of the pull-up switch, and the voltage across C will increase from 0 to VDD. Denoting by iD(t) the charging current supplied by VDD, we can write for the instantaneous power drawn from VDD the expression pDD(t)=VDDiD(t). The energy delivered by the power supply to charge the capacitor can be determined by integrating pDD(t) over the charging interval Tc, EDD=VDD∫0TciD(t)dt=VDDQ where Q is the charge delivered to the capacitor during the charging interval. Since the initial charge on C was zero, Q=CVDD.

Quoted · p. 1176

Thus,

EDD=CVDD2
(17.34)

Since at the end of the charging process the energy stored on the capacitor is

Estored=12CVDD2
(17.35)

we can find the energy dissipated in the pull-up switch as

Edissipated=EDD−Estored=12CVDD2
(17.36)

This energy is dissipated in the on-resistance of switch PU and is converted to heat. Next consider the situation when vI goes high. … Thus all of the energy initially stored on the capacitor, 12CVDD2, will be dissipated in the pull-down switch,

Edissipated=12CVDD2
(17.37)

Thus in each cycle of inverter switching, an amount of energy of 12CVDD2 is dissipated in the pull-up switch and 12CVDD2 is dissipated in the pull-down switch, for a total energy loss per cycle of

Edissipated/cycle=CVDD2
(17.38)

If the inverter is switched at a frequency of f Hz, the dynamic power dissipation of the inverter will be

Pdyn=fCVDD2
(17.39)

This is a general expression that does not depend on the inverter circuit details or the values of the on-resistance of the switches.

Expansion note: energy versus power

Energy is an amount (joules) spent in one charge-discharge cycle. Power is energy per second (watts). Switching f times per second multiplies the energy per cycle by f, which is how Eq. (17.39) follows from Eq. (17.38).

Expansion note: why the supply provides twice what the capacitor stores

The supply delivers CVDD2 while charging, but only half of that is left on the capacitor. The other half is lost as heat in the pull-up switch, and the stored half is lost as heat in the pull-down switch when the capacitor is discharged.
